Your scenario, explained

Where Norway stands, autumn 2026

Inflation is the main problem. Prices rose 3.4% in the year to September, and core inflation (CPI-ATE) 3.0% (SSB). Annual inflation has been above the 2% target every year since 2021. Norges Bank raised the policy rate to 4.50% in September and expects inflation to reach 2% only in 2029.

Growth is weak but positive. SSB expects mainland growth of 1.4% in 2026 and 2.1% in 2027. The Finance Ministry is more cautious (1.1% and 1.7%) and expects CPI inflation to fall from 3.3% to 2.7%. LFS unemployment rose to 5.0% in September (4.7% a year earlier), while NAV registered unemployment is 2.0% (59,413 people).

The krone has strengthened (SSB expects 6.2% on the import-weighted index in 2026), which slowly lowers import prices. Oil prices have been high in 2026 (SSB assumes $89, up from $68 in 2025), keeping petroleum income strong: about NOK 671 bn to the state this year (Norwegianpetroleum.no). The current-account surplus is forecast at 20% of GDP.

The fund keeps growing. NBIM valued it at NOK 22,014 billion on 30 September 2026, about NOK 3.9 million per resident. The 2027 budget proposal uses NOK 608.4 bn of oil money, 2.7% of the fund, below the 3% rule, and the government calls the budget neutral for activity.

Politics and its economic effects

Government: Labour (Ap) under Jonas Gahr Støre governs alone as a minority, after the Centre Party left in January 2025. Labour won the 8 September 2025 election with 28.0%, ahead of the Progress Party (FrP, 23.8%, up from 11.6%) and the Conservatives (H, 14.6%, down from 20.4%). Official results from SSB:

Budget 2027: To pass it, Labour needs SV, the Red Party, the Greens and the Centre Party. The draft cuts income taxes by over NOK 6 bn (lower social-security contributions), raises the wealth-tax threshold slightly, adds NOK 6.5 bn for defence, lifts the fixed electricity price (Norgespris) from 50 to 56 øre/kWh, cuts the VAT exemption for electric cars and halves postal funding. The government calls the budget neutral for activity, which matters while Norges Bank fights inflation.

Opinion has shifted: October 2026 opinion polls (not official results; PolitPro average) put FrP around 31%, Labour around 21% and the Conservatives around 13%. The next Storting election is due in 2029. A right-leaning majority would likely push for lower taxes and fuel duties and stricter immigration; the left-of-centre parties favour higher wealth taxes and faster climate transition. Both directions have budget and fund-spending implications that the simulator can test.

Hot topics: electricity prices and links to Europe, the wealth tax and business owners moving abroad, defence spending and NATO targets, immigration and integration, postal and rural services, and the pace of the oil and gas transition.

The long-term challenges

1. An ageing population. 959,633 people are 67+ (17%). SSB expects people over 65 to outnumber those under 20 in the early 2030s, and the 80+ share to almost double to 9.5% by 2050. More pensions and health care, fewer workers per pensioner.

2. Record-low birth rates. 1.48 children per woman in 2025, up from 1.40 in 2023 but far below the 2.1 replacement level and the 1.98 of 2009. From around 2046, SSB expects more deaths than births; immigration alone will then drive population growth.

3. Many outside work. 374,900 people (10.5% of 18–67) receive disability benefit and 169,300 (4.7%) receive work assessment allowance. Together that is about one in seven of working age (NAV).

4. An integration gap. 21.8% of residents are immigrants or Norwegian-born to immigrant parents (SSB), up from 6.3% in 2000. Immigrants' employment rate is about 12 percentage points below the rest of the population (down from 14 in 2015, IMDi), and recent refugee arrivals, mainly from Ukraine, are still early in the introduction programme.

5. Petroleum decline. Petroleum and ocean shipping were 20% of GDP in 2025 and crude oil and gas 44% of all exports (SSB), but SSB forecasts petroleum investment to fall 4% in 2027 and 6% in 2028. Without new export industries the trade surplus shrinks steadily in the 2030s.

6. Fund dependence and slow productivity. The NOK 608 bn of oil money in 2027 is roughly 13% of mainland GDP. If fund returns disappoint or spending grows faster than the fund, room for welfare narrows; lasting gains must come from higher productivity.

How Norway could improve: options and trade-offs

These are policy options widely discussed by the OECD, IMF, Norway's Productivity Commission and the political parties. Each has trade-offs; parties weigh them differently. Try them in the Simulator with the levers shown.

How the model works

The baseline is the official outlook: SSB's forecast of 15 September 2026 for 2026–2029, the National Budget 2027 for the fund, and gradual convergence to long-run values (1.5% growth, 2% inflation, 4% unemployment) to 2035.

Levers create deviations from that baseline through a small semi-structural model: an output gap driven by fiscal impulse, interest rates, oil-related investment, the krone and global demand; a Phillips curve with exchange-rate pass-through; Okun's law for unemployment; a Taylor-type rule when Norges Bank reacts; population from births, deaths and migration; and the fund's accounting (returns + petroleum cash flow − budget withdrawals).

It is a tool for exploring, not an official forecast. Coefficients are stylised and calibrated to typical Norwegian estimates.

All historical and current figures come from official sources (Statistics Norway, Norges Bank, NBIM, NAV, IMDi and the Ministry of Finance), listed with table numbers on the right. 2023–2025 national-accounts figures are preliminary and may be revised by SSB.

Model assumptions (not data): the levers' effect sizes, sector sensitivities, the 2030–35 extension of the SSB forecast, baseline net immigration (22,000/yr, the 2025 level), the mortgage margin of 1.4 pp, and the end-2026 fund value implied by the budget's 2.7% (NOK 22,533 bn).
